headline.headline: YAMAMOTO GOES THE DISTANCE AS DODGERS BLUDGEON YANKEES 8-2 IN BRONX OPENER
headline.deck: Ohtani, Grisham power Los Angeles in historic complete-game masterpiece
headline.body:
NEW YORK — Yoshinobu Yamamoto needed 66 major league starts to record his first regular-season complete game, and he chose the grandest possible stage to do it. Before 43,305 fans at Yankee Stadium on Sunday, Yamamoto held New York to four hits across nine innings, leading the Los Angeles Dodgers to an 8-2 victory in the first game of a doubleheader and establishing himself as one of the premier pitchers in baseball.

The Dodgers broke through in the third inning with a two-run frame, then added a run in the fifth before blowing the game open with five runs in the eighth. Shohei Ohtani doubled and factored prominently in the Los Angeles offense, while Trent Grisham launched his 11th home run of the season. Andy Pages and Max Muncy each added doubles as the Dodgers roughed up a Yankee pitching staff that had little answer for the visitors' lineup.

Yamamoto's gem was the story of the afternoon, a methodical, commanding performance that silenced one of baseball's most storied ballparks. The right-hander, who arrived from Japan with enormous expectations, delivered on them fully in the Bronx, setting a tone that reverberated even after Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s eighth-inning homer gave the Yankees a 2-1 win in the nightcap to split the twin bill.

secondary.headline: CONTRERAS CRUSHES NO. 22 AS RED SOX ROUT RAYS 6-1
secondary.deck: Boston bats erupt for six runs across three key innings at Fenway
secondary.body:
BOSTON — William Contreras blasted his 22nd home run of the season and Boston added a solo shot from Jr. as the Red Sox rolled past the Tampa Bay Rays 6-1 Sunday before 32,950 at Fenway Park. Boston scored in the second, third, and fifth innings, building a comfortable lead that Tampa Bay starter Shane McClanahan could not contain.

The Rays managed their lone run in the second inning, but the Red Sox answered immediately with three runs in the bottom of the third to seize control. Doubles by Simpson, Feduccia, and Monasterio kept the Boston offense humming throughout the afternoon, with the game completed in a brisk 2 hours and 25 minutes.

secondary.headline: BEDARD LOCKS UP $75M DEAL AS BLACKHAWKS REBUILD AROUND THEIR STAR
secondary.deck: Five-year extension signals Chicago's belief that its young franchise center is ready
secondary.body:
CHICAGO — Connor Bedard and the Chicago Blackhawks agreed to a five-year, $75 million contract extension, the organization announced Sunday, completing the most consequential move of their ongoing rebuild. The deal, averaging $15 million per season, ties Bedard to Chicago through what figures to be the prime years of his career and sends an unmistakable message that the Blackhawks intend to compete for Stanley Cup contention sooner rather than later.

Bedard, who entered the league as one of the most heralded prospects in a generation, has steadily grown into the role of franchise centerpiece. With the NHL playoffs continuing into their second round, the Blackhawks are still watching from the outside, but the Bedard extension gives their front office a concrete cornerstone around which to construct a contender. The signing drew immediate reaction across the league, signaling that Chicago is no longer content to simply develop talent and wait.

secondary.headline: METS POUR IT ON EARLY, ROUT PHILLIES 6-1 IN PHILADELPHIA
secondary.deck: New York scores five runs in first two innings to bury the Phillies at home
secondary.body:
PHILADELPHIA — The New York Mets wasted no time Sunday, scoring two runs in the first inning and three more in the second to build an insurmountable early lead, then coasted to a 6-1 victory over the Philadelphia Phillies before 40,132 at Citizens Bank Park. Carlos Pérez earned the win on the mound as the Mets delivered a statement in the division rivalry.

The Phillies, unable to recover from the early deficit, managed only a single run in the seventh inning. The Mets added an insurance run in the sixth and held firm the rest of the way, completing the game in 3 hours and 6 minutes. The lopsided result extended New York's grip in what has become an increasingly contentious NL East race as the calendar moves toward the second half of the 2026 season.

column.headline: YAMAMOTO FINALLY SILENCED THE DOUBTERS — AND HE PICKED THE PERFECT PLACE TO DO IT
column.body:
Sixty-six starts. That is how long it took Yoshinobu Yamamoto to finish what he started in a major league regular-season game. Sixty-six starts of bullpen doors opening, of pitch counts being monitored, of the Dodgers protecting their prized investment with bubble wrap and careful arithmetic. Sunday afternoon in the Bronx, all of that caution gave way to something simpler and far more satisfying: a pitcher going out and finishing the job.

Yamamoto did not just complete a game. He completed a game at Yankee Stadium, against a New York lineup that demands respect, in front of more than 43,000 fans who wanted nothing more than to see him fail. That is the measuring stick for a pitcher of his contract and reputation. The Dodgers have always believed the investment was worth it. After Sunday, the rest of baseball has no argument left to make.

story.headline: YAMAMOTO DEALS, CHISHOLM DECIDES: DODGERS AND YANKEES SPLIT BRONX TWIN BILL
story.deck: Yoshinobu Yamamoto throws a complete-game gem, but Jazz Chisholm Jr. has the last word.
story.body:
NEW YORK — Yoshinobu Yamamoto finally got his complete game, and it looked for all the world like the Los Angeles Dodgers were going to walk out of Yankee Stadium with a doubleheader sweep. Then Jazz Chisholm Jr. stepped to the plate in the eighth inning of the nightcap, and the Bronx crowd of 43,378 had something to celebrate. Chisholm's 14th home run of the season broke a 1-1 tie and lifted New York to a 2-1 victory, giving the Yankees a split of the July 19 twinbill before 43,305 fans had watched Yamamoto dominate in the afternoon.

In the opener, Yamamoto was a revelation, spinning a four-hitter across nine innings in just his first complete game across 66 major league starts. The Dodgers piled up an 8-2 advantage, detonating for five runs in the eighth inning alone. Trent Grisham launched his 11th homer, Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages each doubled, and Los Angeles stranded 17 men on base while still doing enough damage to cruise. Dodger starter Yamamoto needed no such help, retiring Yankee hitters with methodical efficiency through nine.

The nightcap was a different animal entirely. New York struck first with a run in the first inning and nursed that lead until Tommy Edman — pinch-hitting for Miguel Rojas — answered with his second homer to knot the game at one in the eighth. The Yankees answered immediately, and it was Chisholm's blast off the bullpen that settled matters. Winning pitcher E. Henriquez held Los Angeles to one run over his portion of the contest as the Yankees stranded a staggering 21 runners but found the one swing that mattered most.

story.headline: LENDEBORG LIFTS GOLDEN STATE TO SUMMER LEAGUE CROWN, OUTSHINES BOOZER IN TITLE GAME
story.deck: Yaxel Lendeborg becomes just the second player to win back-to-back summer league MVP honors.
story.body:
LAS VEGAS — Yaxel Lendeborg put on a show under the Thomas & Mack Center lights Sunday, powering the Golden State Warriors to their second NBA Summer League championship with a dominant performance that left Cameron Boozer and the opposition in the dust. Lendeborg, the versatile big man whose relentless motor and scoring instincts drew comparisons to Warriors greats before he ever played a regular-season minute, finished the title game with a tournament-best performance that cemented his status as the crown jewel of Golden State's rebuilding effort.

The victory marks the Warriors' second summer league title in franchise history, and Lendeborg achieved the rare distinction of becoming just the second player ever to claim the tournament's most outstanding player recognition in back-to-back summers. Cameron Boozer, the highly touted prospect who generated buzz throughout the Las Vegas event, could not match Lendeborg's physicality in the paint or his ability to create offense off the dribble when the game was on the line. The Warriors' front office, which has watched the franchise transition away from the Stephen Curry dynasty era, will point to Sunday's result as evidence that the rebuild is ahead of schedule.

For Golden State coach Steve Kerr and his development staff, Lendeborg's emergence offers a genuine reason for optimism heading into the 2026-27 regular season. The summer league title does not guarantee regular-season success, as history repeatedly reminds franchises across the league, but a foundational piece performing at this level in July sends a clear message to the rest of the Western Conference. Warriors fans, starved for winning basketball since the dynasty's twilight, finally have a name worth remembering come October.

story.headline: BEDARD INKS $75M DEAL AS BLACKHAWKS BET BIG ON THEIR FRANCHISE CORNERSTONE
story.deck: Chicago locks up Connor Bedard for five years as Blues and Flyers also make major moves.
story.body:
The Chicago Blackhawks removed all doubt about their rebuilding trajectory Monday, signing star center Connor Bedard to a five-year, $75 million contract that signals the franchise is ready to compete. The deal, worth $15 million per season, keeps the 20-year-old phenom in Chicago through the prime of his career and gives the long-suffering Blackhawks faithful a centerpiece to build their hopes around heading into the 2026-27 season.

The Blackhawks were not alone in making headlines across the league. The St. Louis Blues locked up recently acquired forward Connor McMichael on a six-year, $40.5 million deal, betting that the 24-year-old can provide consistent offensive production alongside an already potent Blues attack. McMichael, who averaged better than 20 goals per season with Washington before his trade to St. Louis, now has the long-term security and the roster around him to take the next step in his development.

In Philadelphia, the Flyers shored up their blue line by signing defenseman Jamie Drysdale to a four-year, $26 million contract. The 23-year-old brings puck-moving ability and offensive instincts to a Philadelphia defensive corps that struggled at times last season. With fantasy hockey analysts already slotting Nathan MacKinnon and Connor McDavid at the top of their 2026-27 preseason rankings, the rest of the league is clearly scrambling to close the gap before October.

story.headline: QUARTERBACK CAROUSEL SPINS WILDLY AS NFL TEAMS RESHAPE ROSTERS FOR 2026
story.deck: Several franchises are gambling big on new signal-callers this spring.
story.body:
The ink is barely dry on the Super Bowl LX confetti, and already the NFL's offseason has produced more drama than most regular seasons. The Cleveland Browns made the boldest splash of the spring, reportedly agreeing to a four-year, $192 million contract with free agent quarterback Sam Darnold, betting that a change of scenery and a rebuilt offensive line can finally unlock the potential scouts saw in him nearly a decade ago. Meanwhile, the New Orleans Saints shipped veteran starter Derek Carr to the Las Vegas Raiders in a stunning reunion trade that sent a second-round pick heading back to New Orleans.

The 2026 NFL Draft, held last month in Washington D.C., delivered its own share of surprises. The Tennessee Titans held the first overall pick and selected Heisman Trophy winner Marcus Webb, a dual-threat quarterback out of Miami, drawing comparisons to a young Lamar Jackson from scouts across the league. The New York Giants traded up six spots to grab Webb's college teammate, wide receiver Darius Polk, a move that had head coach Brian Daboll grinning at the podium. Analysts at the NFL Network called it one of the deepest receiver classes in a generation.

Training camp storylines are already taking shape with rosters in flux. The Dallas Cowboys remain embroiled in a contract holdout situation with star pass rusher Micah Parsons, whose representatives have yet to reach a long-term agreement despite months of negotiations. In New England, rookie head coach Jerod Mayo enters his second full offseason attempting to rebuild the Patriots around youth and athleticism after a modest 2025 campaign. League observers note that the conference balance has rarely looked more competitive heading into a summer of two-a-days.
